output.brief: The evidence points mainly to Callerby's own decision to send the tower crane to Kestrel, not to Halden's architect. The platform's tamper-proof audit trail shows the architect answered 62 of 64 RFIs on time, with a median of 4 working days. The 41 "late" RFIs in the draft claim were measured from when Callerby opened a draft, and 39 of them sat in Callerby's own draft status for 9–47 days. The frame was on hold from October to April with steel on the ground and only 9–14 people on site. Work restarted in April, when the crane came back. Callerby's own report called the crane move a "design hold". The diaries never say what design information was missing. How much delay the change orders caused is still unproven, and so is the claim that the incentive scheme drove the crane move. Don't send the claim as drafted: its RFI basis is contradicted, and Fenmore's fee depends on recovery. Don't concede fully yet either. Commission an independent delay analysis that uses the platform audit data, the crane ledger and the change-order dates, and that separates change-order delay from the crane absence. Don't discipline the superintendent. He answered a direct question truthfully, and a warning would discourage people from speaking up. Leave the incentive scheme as it is until its role is established. Confidence is moderate.
